WITH posted AS (                       -- payments that reached the feed
  SELECT payment_id, sender_id, created_at, audience_override
  FROM p2p_payments
  WHERE status = 'completed'
), resolved AS (                       -- one audience per payment
  SELECT po.payment_id, po.created_at,
         COALESCE(po.audience_override,
                  (SELECT s.default_audience
                   FROM feed_settings s
                   WHERE s.user_id = po.sender_id AND s.changed_at <= po.created_at
                   ORDER BY s.changed_at DESC, s.change_id DESC
                   LIMIT 1),
                  {{initial_sql}}) AS audience
  FROM posted po
)
SELECT date_trunc('month', created_at AT TIME ZONE 'UTC')::date                              AS month,
       COUNT(*)                                                                             AS payments,
       ROUND(COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE audience = 'public')::numeric  / COUNT(*), 4)           AS public_share,
       ROUND(COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE audience = 'friends')::numeric / COUNT(*), 4)           AS friends_share,
       ROUND(COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE audience = 'private')::numeric / COUNT(*), 4)           AS private_share
FROM resolved
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY 1;

{{initial_sql}} is NULL at Medium (every sender has an earlier row) and the instance's initial default, e.g. 'friends', at Hard and Very Hard; a candidate writes the literal. The audience_edits table of Very Hard is deliberately unused.

Explanation. The grain is the payment, so the query first resolves exactly one audience per payment and only then aggregates. Precedence is written once with COALESCE: the override chosen on the payment, else the sender's default in force at created_at, else this exercise's initial default. "In force" is an as-of lookup: the sender's latest setting row at or before the payment, with change_id breaking a tie between two rows at the same second. The initial default sits in the COALESCE, not in a join, so payments made before the sender's first setting row are kept. Declined payments never reached the feed and are filtered before anything else. Later edits change what a payment shows today, not what it was posted with, so they are ignored.

Complexity. One correlated lookup per payment; with an index on feed_settings (user_id, changed_at DESC, change_id DESC) each is a single index probe, O(p log s). A set-based alternative builds validity ranges with LEAD(changed_at) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY changed_at, change_id) and range-joins valid_from <= created_at < valid_to; at scale both become a sort-merge "as-of" join per user.

Dialect notes (described, not executed). Snowflake: ASOF JOIN … MATCH_CONDITION (p.created_at >= s.changed_at) expresses the lookup directly; DIV0; COUNT_IF. BigQuery: no as-of join; use the LEAD validity ranges or ARRAY_AGG(… ORDER BY changed_at DESC LIMIT 1)[OFFSET(0)] in a correlated subquery; COUNTIF; DATE_TRUNC(DATE(created_at), MONTH). Spark SQL: validity ranges and a range join, or max_by(default_audience, struct(changed_at, change_id)) over joined rows. MySQL 8: the correlated ORDER BY … LIMIT 1 works; no FILTER, so SUM(audience = 'public').

Edge cases built into the data. Every level: overrides that differ from the default; senders whose setting changed several times during the quarter; payments in the last seconds of July and the first seconds of August. Hard: declined payments; two senders whose first setting row comes after some of their payments (initial default); a setting changed at exactly a payment's created_at (in force). Very Hard: two rows of one user at the same changed_at followed by a payment (the higher change_id wins), and audience_edits rows that would change the answer if applied.

Common mistakes. Using the sender's current setting; changed_at < created_at; an inner join (or a join on validity ranges without an open-ended last range) that drops payments; ignoring the override, or applying the default over it; counting declined payments; applying later edits; integer division; ties resolved by whatever order the engine returns.

Follow-up guidance. (1) valid_from = changed_at, valid_to = LEAD(changed_at) ordered by (changed_at, change_id), half-open [valid_from, valid_to), NULL valid_to meaning open-ended; rows at the same second produce an empty range for the earlier one, which is correct and harmless with a half-open test. (2) The engine should sort payments and settings by (user_id, time) and merge; a daily snapshot of settings per user is cheaper still when settings change rarely. (3) Keep the posted audience on the payment (immutable) and model edits as an audience history per payment; "currently visible" is the latest edit or the posted value. (4) Join each public payment to the sender's setting changes to private within the 30 days before it; define whether a later switch back counts.

Rubric anchors. 2: shares per month correct only when nothing changed during the quarter (current setting, or no override). 3: matches the expected result. 4: also explains validity ranges, the as-of join at scale and the posted-versus-current distinction.

Strong signals. Asks whether the setting in force or the current setting is wanted before writing SQL; states the precedence as one rule. Red flags. Treating the report as a view of any individual's activity; "just use the latest setting".

WITH current_state AS (                -- one row per transfer: its latest status row
  SELECT DISTINCT ON (transfer_id) *
  FROM transfers
  ORDER BY transfer_id, updated_at DESC
), counted AS (
  SELECT * FROM current_state WHERE status <> 'cancelled'
)
SELECT date_trunc('week', c.sent_at AT TIME ZONE 'UTC')::date                         AS week_start,
       c.send_currency,
       c.receive_currency,
       COUNT(*)                                                                       AS transfers,
       COUNT(c.available_at)                                                          AS available,
       percentile_cont(0.5) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM c.available_at - c.sent_at) / 60)
         FILTER (WHERE c.available_at IS NOT NULL)                                    AS median_minutes,
       ROUND(SUM(c.send_amount_minor)::numeric / power(10::numeric, cs.minor_exponent), cs.minor_exponent) AS sent_total,
       ROUND(COALESCE(SUM(c.receive_amount_minor) FILTER (WHERE c.available_at IS NOT NULL), 0)::numeric
             / power(10::numeric, cr.minor_exponent), cr.minor_exponent)              AS received_total
FROM counted c
JOIN currencies cs ON cs.currency = c.send_currency
JOIN currencies cr ON cr.currency = c.receive_currency
GROUP BY 1, c.send_currency, c.receive_currency, cs.minor_exponent, cr.minor_exponent
ORDER BY 1, 2, 3;

Explanation. First fix the grain: at Very Hard the table is a status log, so DISTINCT ON keeps each transfer's latest row (at Medium and Hard it is already one row per transfer and the step is harmless). Cancelled transfers are removed after choosing the current state — a transfer that was pending and then cancelled is cancelled. Each measure then has its own population inside one GROUP BY: transfers and sent_total over counted transfers, available, the median and received_total over those with an available_at. Amounts are summed in minor units and scaled once by 10 ^ exponent of their own currency, joined twice, in numeric; nothing is ever converted between currencies. percentile_cont interpolates, so an even count yields the mean of the two middle values, and an empty filtered set yields NULL.

Complexity. A sort for DISTINCT ON (O(r log r) over log rows), two tiny hash joins, and a sort per group for the percentile. Exact medians need the group's values; at scale use a daily pre-aggregate of counts and sums plus an approximate quantile sketch (t-digest, KLL) for speed.

Dialect notes (described, not executed). BigQuery: QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY transfer_id ORDER BY updated_at DESC) = 1; DATE_TRUNC(DATE(sent_at), ISOWEEK) for Monday weeks (WEEK alone starts on Sunday); PERCENTILE_CONT(x, 0.5) OVER (…) is analytic only, or APPROX_QUANTILES; NUMERIC/BIGNUMERIC with POW(10, e). Snowflake: QUALIFY, DATE_TRUNC('week', …) depends on WEEK_START; MEDIAN(); DIV0. Spark SQL: percentile(x, 0.5) is exact and interpolates, percentile_approx does not; date_trunc('week', …) is Monday-based. MySQL 8: no percentile function; a ROW_NUMBER/COUNT window trick finds the middle rows.

Edge cases built into the data. Every level: one corridor with a zero-exponent currency and one with a three-exponent currency; transfers sent on Sunday 23:5x and Monday 00:0x UTC; even and odd counts per group (interpolated medians). Hard: pending transfers (counted, not available), cancelled ones (excluded), and a corridor-week in which nothing is available yet (NULL median, received 0). Very Hard: every transfer has a creation row and a final row; some available transfers are touched again later; cancelled transfers whose earlier row was pending.

Common mistakes. Dividing everything by 100; floating-point money; converting currencies; AVG instead of the median; medians including NULL-available transfers as 0; counting cancelled transfers; received_total over pending transfers; Sunday weeks; counting log rows instead of transfers, or taking the first row.

Follow-up guidance. (1) Convert each transfer once at a rate tied to a timestamp (the quote used, or a stated daily rate), round once with a stated rule in the target currency's exponent, then sum; converting summed totals hides rounding and mixes rates across the week. (2) A p90 or p95 of minutes and the count of transfers over a stated threshold; alert when a corridor-week's p90 exceeds its trailing baseline by a margin with a minimum volume. (3) Upsert a current-state table keyed by transfer_id, applying a row only if its updated_at is newer (a version check), so out-of-order arrivals cannot regress the state. (4) Recompute affected weeks and publish versioned snapshots; mark weeks provisional until late statuses have settled.

Rubric anchors. 2: right counts but money scaled by 100 or medians wrong, or log rows counted. 3: matches the expected result. 4: also handles reporting-currency conversion, tail metrics and out-of-order status rows credibly.

Strong signals. Reads currencies before writing arithmetic; names each column's population. Red flags. "Store amounts as floats in dollars"; converting all corridors into one currency without rates and timestamps.

WITH per_plan AS (                     -- one row per counted plan
  SELECT pl.plan_id, pl.purchase_cents, pl.final_due_date,
         COALESCE(SUM(po.amount_cents), 0)                                   AS paid,
         (MAX(po.paid_at) AT TIME ZONE {{tz_sql}})::date                     AS last_paid_date,
         COUNT(po.payment_id) FILTER (WHERE po.kind = 'extra')               AS extras,
         COALESCE(SUM(po.amount_cents) FILTER (WHERE po.kind = 'extra'), 0)  AS extra_cents
  FROM paylater_plans pl
  LEFT JOIN plan_payments po
    ON po.plan_id = pl.plan_id AND po.status = 'posted'
  WHERE pl.status = 'active'
  GROUP BY pl.plan_id
)
SELECT b.band_id, b.label,
       COUNT(p.plan_id)                                                          AS plans,
       COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE p.paid >= p.purchase_cents)                        AS paid_off,
       COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE p.paid >= p.purchase_cents
                          AND p.last_paid_date < p.final_due_date)               AS paid_off_early,
       ROUND(COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE p.paid >= p.purchase_cents
                                AND p.last_paid_date < p.final_due_date)::numeric
             / NULLIF(COUNT(p.plan_id), 0), 4)                                   AS early_share,
       COALESCE(SUM(p.extras), 0)                                                AS extra_payments,
       COALESCE(SUM(p.extra_cents), 0)                                           AS extra_cents
FROM amount_bands b
LEFT JOIN per_plan p
  ON p.purchase_cents >= b.lower_cents
 AND (b.upper_cents IS NULL OR p.purchase_cents < b.upper_cents)
GROUP BY b.band_id, b.label
ORDER BY b.band_id;

{{tz_sql}} is 'UTC' at Medium and Hard and pl.time_zone at Very Hard (grouping by the primary key pl.plan_id makes the plan's other columns usable). A candidate writes it directly.

Explanation. Two grains, two steps. Per plan: the posted total, the last posted payment's date in the right zone, and the extra payments — with the status = 'posted' condition inside the LEFT JOIN so a plan whose only payments were reversed still appears (with 0 paid). Per band: a range join with an inclusive lower and exclusive upper bound, an open top band, and amount_bands on the left so empty bands survive; COUNT(p.plan_id) counts 0 for them and NULLIF turns the share into NULL. Because the sample never overpays, "paid off" is paid >= purchase_cents and its moment is the last posted payment; early means that payment's date is strictly before the final due date, a local date at Very Hard.

Complexity. One pass over payments with a hash aggregate per plan, then a small range join against a handful of bands: O(p + n·b) with b bands, effectively linear. With many bands, sort plans by amount and bands by lower bound and merge.

Dialect notes (described, not executed). BigQuery: DATE(paid_at, time_zone); COUNTIF; SAFE_DIVIDE; LEFT JOIN with a non-equality condition is allowed. Snowflake: CONVERT_TIMEZONE(time_zone, paid_at)::date; COUNT_IF; DIV0NULL. Spark SQL: to_date(from_utc_timestamp(paid_at, time_zone)); a non-equi LEFT JOIN against a small broadcast band table. MySQL 8: no FILTER, so SUM(CASE …); CONVERT_TZ needs the zone tables loaded; GROUP BY on a primary key also allows the plan's other columns.

Edge cases built into the data. Every level: plans paid on schedule (last payment on the final due date, not early), plans paid off early with an extra payment, plans with small extra payments that still finish on the due date, plans that stopped paying, and an empty top band. Hard: cancelled plans with extra payments; a reversed extra payment that would otherwise have paid a plan off; a reversed duplicate of a scheduled payment; purchases exactly on band lower bounds; last payments at 23:59:xx the day before the due date (early) and 00:00:xx on it (not early). Very Hard: plans in Los Angeles paid at 03:00 UTC on the due date (the day before locally: early) and in Tokyo paid at 22:00 UTC the day before (the due date locally: not early).

Common mistakes. An inner join (or a WHERE on plan columns after the LEFT JOIN) that drops empty bands; BETWEEN bounds; <= against the due date; counting reversed payments or cancelled plans; filtering reversed payments in WHERE after the plan-payment LEFT JOIN, losing plans; aggregating payments straight to bands, which counts plans once per payment; UTC dates at Very Hard; COUNT(*) for plans in a band with none.

Follow-up guidance. (1) Only judge plans whose final due date has passed by the report date (a mature cohort), and show immature plans separately as "paid off so far"; mixing them understates early payoff for recent months. (2) Bands are data: keep band sets versioned (band_set_id, valid dates) and parameterise the report by set; old reports name their set. (3) Model a refund as an adjustment that lowers the amount owed (a schedule version) and define "paid off" against the adjusted amount as of each payment. (4) Keep per-plan state (paid total, last posted payment, extras) updated from each day's payments and reversals; band totals are sums of plan states.

Rubric anchors. 2: correct for paid-off counts but empty bands missing, inclusive due date, or reversed payments counted. 3: matches the expected result. 4: also discusses mature cohorts and versioned bands and keeps the analysis about the product, not about people.

Strong signals. States both grains (plan, band) before writing; asks which time zone a due date is in. Red flags. Interpreting early payoff as a judgement of a consumer's means; presenting the schedule as a real product's terms.

def mutual_payers(payments, window_days, aliases=None):
    aliases = aliases or {}
    W = window_days * 86400
    counted = []
    for pid, sender, recipient, ts, status in payments:
        if status != 'completed':
            continue
        if recipient not in aliases and ':' in recipient:
            continue                       # an identifier nobody has claimed
        recipient = aliases.get(recipient, recipient)
        if recipient == sender:
            continue
        counted.append((ts, pid, sender, recipient))
    counted.sort()
    last = {}                              # (sender, recipient) -> latest ts so far
    out = {}
    for ts, pid, s, r in counted:
        prev = last.get((r, s))
        if prev is not None and ts - prev <= W:
            key = (s, r) if s < r else (r, s)
            got = out.get(key)
            if got is None:
                out[key] = (pid, ts - prev, 1)
            else:
                out[key] = (got[0], got[1], got[2] + 1)
        last[(s, r)] = ts
    return out

Explanation. Normalise first: keep completed payments, resolve identifiers through aliases (dropping unclaimed ones), and drop payments to oneself. Sort once by (ts, payment_id), which is exactly the "earlier" order of the spec. Walking in that order, the dict last holds, for each directed pair, the time of its latest payment so far — so for a payment u → v, last[(v, u)] is the latest earlier payment the other way. If it is within the window the payment reciprocates, and its gap is measured from exactly that payment. The first reciprocating payment of a pair is the first time this fires; later ones only increase the count. Keys are the sorted pair so both directions land on one entry.

Complexity. O(n log n) for the sort and O(n) for the walk, O(n) memory. The timing test (250 000 random payments plus three pairs with 8 000 payments each way, one direction for months and then the other) runs in about 0.5–0.75 s in CPython. Comparing every pair of payments is O(n²) — hours at this size.

The middle approach. The most likely middle solution groups payments by directed pair and, for each pair, compares every payment of one direction with every payment of the other: O(a·b) per pair. On the busy pairs that is 2 × 8 000 × 8 000 comparisons each; it took about 45 s in CPython in our timing, well over the 8 s limit. A per-pair solution that sorts both directions and uses bisect (or two pointers) to find the latest earlier opposite payment is O(n log n) and passes; so does a backward scan from each payment that stops as soon as it leaves the window, because it never looks past the window. Both are acceptable answers.

Dialect notes. Java: HashMap<String, Long> keyed by sender + '\u0000' + recipient, a record for the result, Long.compare sort keys. In SQL the rule is a self-join on (sender, recipient) = (recipient, sender) with p2.ts - p1.ts BETWEEN 0 AND W plus a tie rule on payment_id; for the gap use a correlated MAX. It is correct but the join is O(a·b) for busy pairs unless the engine does a range (interval) join; a window function over the union of both directions ordered by time — LAST_VALUE(CASE WHEN direction = 'back' THEN ts END IGNORE NULLS) — is linear after the sort. Not executed here.

Edge cases built into the tests. Exactly window_days apart (reciprocates) and one second more (does not); one direction only; the gap from the latest earlier opposite payment; the same second in opposite directions (the higher payment_id reciprocates, gap 0); back and forth counting every reciprocating payment, with one outside the window; the key sorted whoever paid first; three users with two pairs; no payments. Hard: unsorted input where list order differs from time order; failed and refunded payments; payments to oneself. Very Hard: an email identifier resolved to its owner, an unclaimed identifier ignored, and a payment to one's own phone identifier ignored.

Common mistakes. Measuring the gap from the first opposite payment instead of the latest; exclusive window; picking the first reciprocating payment by list position; ordered keys (two entries per pair); counting the pair's first payment; resolving identifiers after the self-payment check; treating an unclaimed identifier as a user; per-pair nested loops.

Follow-up guidance. (1) Keep, per directed pair, the amount (or recent amounts) of the latest payment, and define "roughly" as within a stated number of cents or a stated per-mille of the first amount, in integers. (2) Carry last forward, but only entries newer than the window — older ones can never reciprocate again — so the state is bounded by the pairs active in the last window_days. (3) Self-join or window over the union of directions as above; the self-join is the explosive one for busy pairs. (4) Build a graph of reciprocating pairs and look at connected groups or a household-like cluster, reported in aggregate only.

Rubric anchors. 2: correct with per-pair nested loops, or fast but wrong on ties, the gap or unsorted input. 3: all tests pass with one sort and a dict. 4: also explains bounded incremental state, the SQL formulation and keeps pair data private.

Strong signals. Asks what "earlier" means at equal timestamps; normalises before sorting. Red flags. Labelling pairs as relationships or exposing pair data to third parties; inferring anything about people from who pays whom.

from bisect import bisect_left


def balance_targets(opening_cents, events, targets, end_of_day=False):
    dates, peaks = [], []                  # each new running maximum and the date it was set
    bal = opening_cents
    best = opening_cents
    n = len(events)
    for i, (day, cents) in enumerate(events):
        bal += cents
        if end_of_day and i + 1 < n and events[i + 1][0] == day:
            continue                       # only the day's closing balance counts
        if bal > best:
            best = bal
            dates.append(day)
            peaks.append(bal)
    out = []
    for t in targets:
        if t <= opening_cents:
            out.append('opening')
            continue
        k = bisect_left(peaks, t)
        out.append(dates[k] if k < len(peaks) else None)
    return out

Explanation. The balance first reaches t exactly when the running maximum first reaches t, and the running maximum never decreases. Recording only the moments it strictly rises gives a strictly increasing list of values with their dates; bisect_left returns the first value at least t, whose date is the answer. Targets at or below the opening balance were met before the history began ('opening'); targets above every recorded peak are None. With end_of_day, a balance counts only after the last event of its date, so intraday peaks are skipped before the running maximum sees them.

Complexity. O(n) to build the list and O(log n) per target: O(n + q log n), O(n) memory. The timing test (200 000 events, 20 000 targets, about 40% never reached) runs in about 0.02–0.03 s in CPython, plus building the input.

The middle approach. The most likely middle solution replays the history per target and breaks at the first hit. It is fast for targets reached early, but each of the roughly 8 000 unreached targets reads all 200 000 events: about 145 s in CPython in our timing, far over the 8 s limit. Sorting the targets and sweeping the history once (answering targets in increasing order as the balance passes them, then restoring input order) is O(n + q log q) and passes; it is an acceptable answer.

Dialect notes. Java: long[] peaks and Arrays.binarySearch (adjust its negative insertion point) or a hand-written lower bound. In SQL: MAX(balance) OVER (ORDER BY seq) gives the running maximum; for each target, MIN(date) where the running maximum is at least the target — a range join that a warehouse handles by sorting both sides; end-of-day uses the last row per date (ROW_NUMBER() … DESC = 1) first. Not executed here.

Edge cases built into the tests. A balance exactly equal to the target and one cent short; a peak that falls back (still reached on its date); the first date rather than a later, higher one; a target above every balance; no events; targets out of order. Hard: a target equal to the opening balance ('opening'), a dip below the opening balance, repeated targets. Very Hard: an intraday peak spent the same day (reaches nothing), a closing balance that reaches a target after a dip during the day, and several events on the last date.

Common mistakes. Bisecting the raw balances (not sorted); appending equal peaks so bisect_left returns a later date; strict comparison; returning None or the first date for targets met by the opening balance; checking intraday balances in end-of-day mode; answering targets in sorted order rather than input order; a per-target replay.

Follow-up guidance. (1) Appending events only appends peaks; answers already given never change, and a cached None can become a date. (2) A reversal before the end changes every balance after it: rebuild the peak list from the restated event onwards (everything before is unchanged); a segment tree of (sum, maximum prefix) supports point updates in O(log n) if restatements are frequent. (3) "At least t for 30 consecutive days" is a run-length question over daily closing balances; for many targets, process targets in decreasing order with a structure of maximal runs (or offline with a union of days as the threshold falls). (4) Balances in different currencies cannot be added without a stated conversion; refuse a single "500" across currencies or define the reporting currency, rate and rounding explicitly.

import heapq


def settle_group(members, expenses, repaid, currencies, home, remainder):
    joined = {m: i for i, m in enumerate(members)}
    bal = dict.fromkeys(members, 0)
    e_home = currencies[home][0]
    for payer, amount, code, parts in expenses:
        if code != home:
            e, num, den = currencies[code]
            top = amount * num * 10 ** e_home
            bottom = den * 10 ** e
            amount = (2 * top + bottom) // (2 * bottom)       # half up, once, before the split
        bal[payer] += amount
        share, left = divmod(amount, len(parts))
        order = parts if remainder == "listed" else sorted(parts, key=joined.__getitem__)
        for i, m in enumerate(order):
            bal[m] -= share + (1 if i < left else 0)
    for a, b, x in repaid:
        bal[a] += x
        bal[b] -= x

    creditors = [(-v, joined[m], m) for m, v in bal.items() if v > 0]   # largest first, then joined first
    debtors = [(v, joined[m], m) for m, v in bal.items() if v < 0]      # most negative first
    heapq.heapify(creditors)
    heapq.heapify(debtors)
    out = []
    while creditors and debtors:
        c, ci, cm = heapq.heappop(creditors)
        d, di, dm = heapq.heappop(debtors)
        x = min(-c, -d)
        out.append((dm, cm, x))
        if -c > x:
            heapq.heappush(creditors, (c + x, ci, cm))
        if -d > x:
            heapq.heappush(debtors, (d + x, di, dm))
    return out

Balances are one pass: convert an expense once (Very Hard), split it with divmod so the shares add up exactly, and give the leftover units to the first participants by the stated order; repayments move both balances. Settlement then repeats one step: the largest creditor and the most negative debtor, ties to the earlier join index, transfer the smaller of the two magnitudes. The heap keys (−balance, join index) and (balance, join index) encode the rule and the tie exactly. After a transfer at least one of the two is at zero and is dropped; the other is pushed back with its new balance, so each step is O(log n). Because balances sum to zero, the creditors and debtors run out together.

Complexity. O(Σ participants + n log n) time, O(n) memory. At most n − 1 transfers, since each one clears a member. The timing test (40 000 members, 64 000 expenses, 2 to 6 participants each) runs in about 0.2 to 0.3 s in CPython. Scanning every member for the largest creditor and debtor before each transfer takes about 13 s at 10 000 members and grows with n²; on the timing test itself it was still running when stopped at 120 s.

The middle approach. The likely middle answer keeps one list of non-zero balances and calls sort after every transfer. Timsort is fast on a nearly sorted list (close to O(n) with C comparisons), but it still touches every member per transfer, so it is O(n²) overall: about 16 s at 10 000 members and 83 s at 20 000 in CPython, and on the timing test itself it was still running when stopped at 120 s, far over the 8 s limit. It fails. Two sorted lists maintained with bisect.insort (remove the two, reinsert the survivor) are O(log n) comparisons and O(n) memory moves in C per transfer; at 40 000 members that passes and is an acceptable answer if the candidate states the memmove cost. A balanced tree or a sorted container is also fine.

Dialect notes. In SQL the balances are a GROUP BY over expense shares (the remainder needs ROW_NUMBER() over the participant order) plus repayments; the settlement rule is inherently sequential and is not a natural set-based query (a recursive CTE can do it one transfer per step, which is O(n²)). In Java use two PriorityQueue<long[]> with comparators on balance then join index, and long amounts; the conversion amount × num × 10^e should use long or BigInteger and be checked for overflow. Not executed here.

Edge cases built into the tests. A split with leftover units where listed and join order differ; a payer outside the participants; everyone already even ([]); an expense for the payer alone; equal creditors and equal debtors (join-order ties); one transfer clearing both sides; a group where largest-first makes four transfers although three would do; a member in no expense. Hard adds a repayment, a repayment that overshoots (a debtor becomes a creditor) and leftover units over several expenses. Very Hard adds a conversion landing on exactly half a minor unit (rounds up), three-decimal and zero-decimal currencies, and a conversion that must be rounded once before the split rather than per share.

Common mistakes. Floats for shares (amount / k), so shares do not add up; giving the remainder to the payer or to the last participant; forgetting the payer's own share; ties by member id instead of join order; "optimising" to fewer transfers, which breaks the stated rule; converting per share; using an exponent of 2 for every currency; a min-heap of creditors keyed on +balance; pushing back both members after a transfer, including one at zero.

(2) The example in the tests: balances +4, +3, +2, −5, −4. Largest-first makes four transfers; {+3, +2, −5} and {+4, −4} make three. The fewest transfers equals n minus the largest number of disjoint zero-sum groups, which is NP-hard in general (it contains subset sum). (4) Recompute balances incrementally (each expense touches only its participants); keep paid transfers as repayments; a stable plan matters to users, so present a new plan as a delta and recompute only on request.

def lowest_balance(opening, arrivals):
    # Every event's final place in history: by t, then by its first arrival.
    first = {}
    for i, (eid, t, _) in enumerate(arrivals):
        if eid not in first:
            first[eid] = (t, i)
    order = sorted(first, key=first.__getitem__)
    slot = {eid: p for p, eid in enumerate(order)}
    when = [first[eid][0] for eid in order]

    size = 1
    while size < len(order):
        size *= 2
    INF = float("inf")
    total = [0] * (2 * size)         # sum of a node's filled slots
    low = [INF] * (2 * size)         # lowest prefix sum inside the node (INF when empty)
    pos = [-1] * (2 * size)          # slot where that lowest prefix is first reached
    out = []
    for eid, t, amount in arrivals:
        i = size + slot[eid]
        total[i] = low[i] = amount   # a correction simply rewrites the slot
        pos[i] = i - size
        i >>= 1
        while i:
            l = 2 * i
            r = l + 1
            right = total[l] + low[r]
            total[i] = total[l] + total[r]
            if low[l] <= right:      # ties: the earlier (left) event wins
                low[i] = low[l]
                pos[i] = pos[l]
            else:
                low[i] = right
                pos[i] = pos[r]
            i >>= 1
        out.append((opening + low[1], when[pos[1]]))
    return out

Explanation. Running balances are opening plus prefix sums in history order, so the answer is the minimum prefix sum over the filled history. The whole arrival list is known, so every event's final slot is known: sort events by (t, first arrival). A segment tree over the slots keeps, per node, the total of its filled slots and the lowest prefix sum within it; combining left and right gives min(L.low, L.total + R.low). Empty slots have total 0 and low +∞, so they neither move later balances nor become the answer. Each arrival fills or rewrites one leaf and updates log n ancestors; the root holds the answer, and the stored position (left preferred on ties) gives the earliest event with that balance.

Complexity. O(n log n) for the sort plus O(log n) per arrival; O(n) memory. The timing test (80 000 arrivals, 40% back-dated to a random earlier minute) runs in about 0.7 to 0.85 s in CPython with flat lists. Re-sorting and recomputing all balances per arrival takes about 13 s at 20 000 arrivals and grows with n².

The middle approach. The likely middle answer keeps the history in a list (bisect.insort by (t, arrival)), keeps the running balances, and after each arrival recomputes balances only from the inserted position on, then takes min over the list. With C-speed itertools.accumulate and min it is still O(n) per arrival because back-dated events land early: measured at about 5.8 s for 20 000 arrivals, 27 s for 40 000, and about 150 s on the 80 000-arrival timing test (more than 150 s at Very Hard, where corrections add work). It fails by a factor of more than 100. Keeping a prefix-minimum array as well does not help, since every prefix minimum after the insertion point also changes. Square-root decomposition (blocks of about √n events with a total and lowest prefix per block) is O(√n) per arrival and lands near the limit in CPython; accept it with a correct argument, but probe its constant. An online balanced tree (treap) with the same augmentation is a fully acceptable answer and handles follow-up 1.

Dialect notes. In SQL the lowest balance at the end is MIN(SUM(amount) OVER (ORDER BY t, arrival_seq ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING)); the answer "after each arrival" needs one window per arrival, which is the O(n²) recompute. Streaming engines compute it incrementally only for in-order data; back-dated events force a recomputation of the affected range or a tree-like state. In Java the same segment tree with long[] arrays and Long.MAX_VALUE as the empty low (careful: total + Long.MAX_VALUE overflows, so test emptiness explicitly). Not executed here.

Edge cases built into the tests. One event (its balance, not the opening balance); events in time order; a back-dated debit making a new low; a back-dated credit moving the low; an event dated before everything arriving last; equal lows (the earlier event wins), including equal lows created by a late event between them; a balance below zero. Hard adds same-minute events ordered by arrival, and a later arrival at the same minute that is lower. Very Hard adds corrections that rewrite an amount in place, a correction to zero that cancels the low, and a correction of the first event that shifts every later balance.

Common mistakes. Including the opening balance as a candidate; ordering same-minute events by amount or id; inserting a correction as a new event; reporting the latest event on a tie; using 0 instead of +∞ for an empty slot, which makes the low 0 too early; recomputing from the insertion point and calling it O(log n) because of bisect; a recursive tree that rebuilds per arrival.

(2) A range query on the same tree: combine the O(log n) nodes covering the range, carrying the total before the range so prefixes start from the right balance. (3) Keep a tree per account, persisted with checkpoints per period (period total and lowest prefix), so a back-dated event updates one period and the path above it; show the user that a past low changed and why. from datetime import datetime, timedelta, timezone


def _round_half_up(n, d):
    return (2 * n + d) // (2 * d)


def _to_home(amount, code, home, currencies, rates):
    """Minor units of code -> minor units of home, at one cross rate, rounded once."""
    num, den = rates[code]
    hnum, hden = rates[home]
    top = amount * num * hden * 10 ** currencies[home]
    bottom = den * hnum * 10 ** currencies[code]            # the currency's own exponent
    return _round_half_up(top, bottom)


def _local_month(ts, offset_minutes):
    when = datetime.fromisoformat(ts).astimezone(timezone(timedelta(minutes=offset_minutes)))
    return when.strftime("%Y-%m")


def monthly_statement(entries, month, offset_minutes, home, currencies, rates):
    out = {"sent": 0, "received": 0, "net": 0, "from_balance": 0, "from_linked": 0, "reversed": 0}
    reversed_ids = {e["reverses"] for e in entries if e["kind"] == "reversal"}
    for e in entries:
        if e["kind"] == "reversal":
            continue                                          # never counted itself
        if _local_month(e["ts"], offset_minutes) != month:
            continue
        if e["id"] in reversed_ids:
            out["reversed"] += 1                              # in neither total
            continue
        amount = _to_home(e["amount"], e["currency"], home, currencies, rates)
        if e["kind"] == "sent":
            out["sent"] += amount
            for source, outcome in e["funding"]:
                if outcome != "used":
                    continue                                  # a declined attempt moved no money
                if source == "balance":
                    out["from_balance"] += amount
                else:
                    out["from_linked"] += amount
        else:
            out["received"] += amount
    out["net"] = out["received"] - out["sent"]
    return out

The planted bugs, their symptoms and their fixes.

  1. Every currency assumed to have two decimals. _to_home divides by 10 ** 2 instead of 10 ** currencies[code]. Symptom: yen amounts (0 decimals) come out a hundred times too small, dinar amounts (3 decimals) ten times too large; dollar, euro and pound amounts are right, so it hides in most data. Fix: use the source currency's exponent.
  2. Rounded twice. The amount is first rounded to US cents, then converted to the home currency and rounded again. Symptom: when neither currency is the US dollar, some amounts are a minor unit off the one-step conversion shown to the user. Fix: one cross-rate expression, rounded once.
  3. Reversals counted as payments. Every non-sent entry, reversals included, is added to received, reversed payments are kept, and reversed stays 0. Symptom: a reversed payment inflates both totals (the net hides it); a payment reversed next month still counts. Fix: collect reversed ids over all entries, skip reversal entries, skip and count reversed payments.
  4. The month relabels UTC. replace(tzinfo=…) attaches the offset to the UTC wall-clock time instead of converting, so the month is always the UTC month. Symptom: a California user's evening payment on 30 September appears in October; a Sydney user's morning payment on 1 November appears in October. Fix: astimezone.
  5. Funding fallbacks counted twice. The funding loop adds the amount for every attempt, declined ones included. Symptom: a payment that fell back from the balance to a card is counted in both from_balance and from_linked, which then exceed sent. Fix: count only the used attempt.

Each bug has its own checks, and fixing one bug turns exactly its checks green (verified by fixing each alone): a yen and a dinar entry with home US dollars (bug 1); euros into pounds at an amount where the two roundings differ (bug 2); a payment reversed in the same month and one reversed next month (bug 3); 02:00 UTC on the 1st for a user west of UTC and 22:00 UTC on the last day for a user east of UTC (bug 4); a balance declined then a card used (bug 5). The plain US-dollar check and the other-month check pass on the original code and stay as regression checks. Random samples can hit several bugs at once.

Explanation. A statement is three decisions per entry: does it belong to this month (converted to the user's offset, and not reversed), how much is it in the home currency (one exact conversion with each currency's exponent), and where does it go (sent or received, and the used funding source). Each bug breaks one of them.

  • Events.   • Authority. Money outcomes come only from server attempts and payment_finished; what the user saw comes only from client screens. Silent fallbacks are attempts with no matching screen.
  • Pipeline. Server events are produced transactionally with the payment write (an outbox) so none are lost. Client events go through the collection endpoint, deduplicated on client_event_id. A stream job builds fact_funding_attempt and fact_payment_funding (payment_id, attempts, first_source_kind, used_source_kind, fallback bool, silent_fallback bool, user_cancelled bool, total_latency_ms, status, day) and joins screens with an allowed lateness of {{late_hours}} hours; daily partitions are rewritten when late screens arrive, and a day is marked final after the lateness window.

  • Reports. Decline rate per source kind and category (denominator: attempts), fallback success (denominator: payments with a fallback), user-visible fallback rate, time to complete, cancellations at the prompt; all aggregates by client, country and day.

All fine if order, authority, deduplication, lateness and reconciliation are explicit.

Card details leaking through error payloads; client retries doubling screens; attempts without a payment id; clock skew between client and server; changing decline categories; denominators mixed between attempts and payments; late events rewriting old partitions forever.

AND state='open' AND now() < expires_at, using server time; zero rows updated means expired or already used, and the client is shown a fresh quote. Client retries carry the same quote id, so a second acceptance is a no-op that returns the first result.
  • Conversion record. conversion (conversion_id, quote_id, payment_id, send_amount_minor, receive_amount_minor, applied_rate, created_at), written in the same transaction as the acceptance, with applied_rate and amounts copied from the quote; a check constraint or validation recomputes the amount from the stored inputs.
  • Proof and reconciliation. A daily job joins every conversion to its quote and verifies: quote exists, accepted before expiry, single use, applied rate and amounts equal, recomputation from inputs matches. Exceptions go to a queue with the payment id. Quote and conversion tables are append-only with change history; the audit set (accepted quotes and their conversions) is kept {{audit_years}} years, with hashes or signed daily manifests for tamper evidence.
  • Unaccepted quotes. At {{daily_quotes}} a day most are never used: keep them in full for a short window (for disputes about what was shown), then aggregate to pair, hour, shown, accepted, expired, mean margin, and drop the rows.
  • Rate sets. The upstream feed is ingested as versioned rate sets; each quote references its version, so a bad set can be traced to every quote and conversion that used it.

Competing designs to accept. A signed quote token held by the client and verified on acceptance (accept if single use is enforced server-side); an event-sourced quote log; storing only accepted quotes plus aggregates (accept if the "what was shown" question can still be answered for the dispute window).

Bottlenecks and failure modes. Floats for rates; rounding twice or with the wrong exponent; client clocks deciding expiry; quotes in a cache without a durable record; double acceptance from two devices; bad upstream rates; unbounded growth of unaccepted quotes.

Incident guidance.

  • A rate off by a factor of 100: stop quoting from that rate-set version, find every quote issued from it (by rate_set_version and pair) and every conversion accepted from those quotes, measure the money impact per currency, decide remediation by policy, and add a jump-limit check per pair before a rate set reaches quoting.
  • Client time used for expiry: revert to server time, list acceptances where server receive time was after expires_at, quantify the market difference the business carried, and add a reconciliation rule that flags any conversion accepted after its quote's expiry.

Follow-up guidance. (1) Query by rate_set_version and pair; conversions join through quote_id; measure the money impact per currency. (2) Produce the quote as shown (rate, amounts, expiry), the acceptance time against expiry, the conversion record, and a recomputation from stored inputs; show that the applied rate equals the quoted rate. (3) The business carries the market move between issue and acceptance; build a table of quoted rate versus market rate at acceptance per pair and hour, and set the lifetime per pair from it. (4) Tier unaccepted quotes to aggregates after the dispute window; keep accepted quotes and conversions in compressed, partitioned storage for {{audit_years}} years.

Rubric anchors. 2: rates in a cache only, client-side expiry, or floats. 3: immutable quotes, atomic single-use acceptance on server time, conversions linked to quotes, one rounding with exponents from data. 4: also rate-set versioning, recomputation-based proof, differentiated retention and a clear plan for a bad upstream rate.

Strong signals. Asks whose clock decides expiry and where rounding happens; stores inputs, not only outputs. Red flags. "We recompute the rate at settlement"; storing quotes only in a cache.

PYP-L3-01.html:
Reference architecture (one defensible design; score others on the criteria).

  • Reference data. currencies (currency, exponent) with exponent 0, 2 or 3; every amount column is BIGINT in minor units next to a currency column, and display formatting reads the exponent from here.
  • Accounts and instruments. accounts (account_id, user_id, home_country, opened_at, closed_at). instruments (instrument_id, kind bank|card, token, display_suffix, network_or_bank_ref, currency); the token comes from a vault and no card or bank number exists in this model. instrument_links (link_id, account_id, instrument_id, linked_at, verified_at NULL, removed_at NULL, removed_reason): relinking the same instrument is a new link row, so history is never overwritten.
  • Preference history. funding_preferences (account_id, instrument_id NULL, balance_first bool, valid_from, valid_to NULL), non-overlapping per account (an exclusion constraint on a range, or a single writer that closes the previous row in the same transaction). Removing the preferred instrument closes the preference interval with a reason; "preferred on D" is the interval containing D, possibly "none".
  • Balances from movements. balance_movements (movement_id, account_id, currency, bucket available|held, amount_minor signed, kind payment_debit|payment_credit|hold_placed|hold_released|conversion_out|conversion_in|refund, payment_id NULL, hold_id NULL, conversion_id NULL, occurred_at, recorded_at). A hold is two movements per side: placed (available −x, held +x) and released (held −x, available +x). Available at T = Σ available-bucket movements with occurred_at <= T; held likewise. balance_snapshots (account_id, currency, as_of, available_minor, held_minor) daily (or every N movements) so an as-of read is a snapshot plus a short tail; the snapshot is rebuildable.
  • Holds. holds (hold_id, account_id, currency, amount_minor, placed_at, release_due_at, released_at NULL, review_ref); release_due_at at most {{hold_days}} days after placement in this exercise; the review is only referenced.
  • Conversions. conversions (conversion_id, account_id, from_currency, to_currency, from_minor, to_minor, rate, quote_id, quoted_at, applied_at, rounding_rule), rounded once, half away from zero, to the target's minor unit.
  • Funding legs. payment_funding_legs (payment_id, leg_no, source_kind balance|bank|card, currency_of_source, instrument_id NULL, source_minor, payment_minor, conversion_id NULL, attempt_outcome used|declined, decline_reason NULL). Invariant: Σ payment_minor over used legs = payment amount; declined attempts are kept with zero amounts for the funding-mix and fallback questions. Refunds write refund_legs (refund_id, payment_id, leg_no, minor) reversing legs in reverse order (this exercise's rule).
  • Analytics. fct_funding_leg_daily (date, payment_currency, source_kind, legs, payments, payment_minor_sum) built from legs, never from accounts; shares by amount are Σ leg amount ÷ Σ payment amount, so they add up to 100%.
  • Concurrency. The write path serialises per (account, currency): a row lock on a per-balance row holding the derived current available amount, updated in the same transaction as the movement with a CHECK (available_minor >= 0), or a conditional update (… WHERE available_minor >= :x). The cached figure is a derived lock target, rebuilt from movements and reconciled daily.

Competing designs to accept. A double-entry journal underneath (accept, as long as the candidate keeps the wallet questions in view: funding legs, preference history, per-currency available and held). Holds as a separate table with available computed as Σ balance − Σ open holds, if "available at T" still works for past T. An event-sourced account aggregate with the balance row as its projection. Per-payment funding stored as JSON on the payment, if they show how the funding mix is computed and reconciled.

Bottlenecks and failure modes. One balance column per user; balance in one currency only; a float or decimal amount with an assumed exponent; instrument rows overwritten on removal; a preferred flag with no history; holds as a boolean on the payment; funding recorded as a single source per payment; conversions rounded per leg and again on the total; funding mix counted by payments rather than by leg amounts; balance checks against a cached value read outside the transaction; at {{payments_per_day}} payments a day, as-of balance queries that scan all movements.

Incident guidance.

  • Funding mix over 100%: payments with two sources were counted once per source. Recompute the daily fact from legs by amount (and, if a count is wanted, count legs and payments separately with clear labels); add a test that shares by amount add up to 100% per day and currency.
  • Negative available balance: a check-then-write race on a cached balance. Move the check into the write transaction (row lock or conditional update, with a non-negative constraint), find the affected accounts from movements, and resolve each negative window by the rule the product sets (for example, holding the later payment); alert on any negative derived balance.
  • Statement totals moving daily: conversion at read time with current rates. Use the rate recorded on each conversion or leg; where a cross-currency total is only informative, label it with the rate date and freeze it with the statement. Restate the affected statements and add a check that a closed statement's totals never change.

Follow-up guidance. (1) Snapshot at or before T plus Σ movements in (snapshot, T], per bucket; index (account_id, currency, occurred_at). (2) Leg 1: balance 1840 EUR minor; leg 2: card in USD with a conversion row, payment_minor 3160 EUR; check Σ payment_minor = 5000. (3) The preference interval was closed on the 3rd (reason: instrument removed), so on the 5th no instrument was preferred; a payment on the 5th used the balance and then the fallback rule, and its legs say so. (4) Facts: movements and funding legs at event grain; daily fact by date, currency and source kind; incremental by date partition. (5) Serialise per balance; the second payment fails or uses the next source, never goes negative.

Rubric anchors. 2: a users table with a balance column and a default card flag; floats; no history. 3: instruments and links over time, preference history, per-currency movements with available and held, funding legs that reconcile. 4: also conversions recorded once with the shown rate, refunds against legs, write-path concurrency, rebuildable snapshots sized for volume, and incident repairs.

Strong signals. Writes the leg invariant unprompted; asks where the exponent comes from; treats the cached balance as derived. Red flags. Storing card numbers; amounts in floating point; overwriting instrument or preference rows; converting historical totals at today's rate.

PYP-L3-02.html:
Reference architecture (one defensible design).

  • Requests. requests (request_id, requester_account_id, kind single|split, currency, created_at, rule_version) and request_versions (request_id, version, total_minor, split_method equal|custom, participants_ordered, created_at): an edit before any payment is a new version, and shares are recomputed for it.
  • Shares. shares (share_id, request_id, version, participant_ref, position, amount_minor, remainder_minor) where participant_ref is an account or an invited identifier. Equal split: base = total ÷ n (integer division), leftover = total − base × n; participants at positions 1..leftover get +1 minor unit (this exercise's rule). Invariant: Σ shares = total for each version, checked on write.
  • Share events. share_events (event_id, share_id, kind paid|declined|expired|cancelled|reminded, amount_minor NULL, payment_id NULL, source_currency NULL, source_minor NULL, conversion_id NULL, occurred_at, recorded_at). A payment answers one share and never exceeds the outstanding amount (checked in the transaction that writes the event).
  • Rules. request_rules (rule_version, reminder_after_hours, expiry_after_days, remainder_rule, valid_from); each request stores the version it was created under, so expiry and reminders use that version. Expiry in this exercise: {{expiry_days}} days under the current version.
  • State as of D. A share's state at T is a fold of its events with occurred_at <= T: outstanding = amount − Σ paid; status open | paid | partly paid | declined | expired | cancelled. A request is settled when every share is paid or declined (say how declines count; see follow-up 4). share_state_daily (date, share_id, outstanding_minor, status) for open shares only is an optimisation, rebuilt for days touched by late events.
  • Reminders. Eligible today: shares open with outstanding > 0, created_at + reminder_after_hours <= now, no reminded event, not cancelled or expired; reminder event keyed by (share_id, reminder_no), so a retry cannot send twice; the job re-reads state at send time.
  • Analytics. fct_request (request_id, created_week, amount_band, participants, settled_at NULL, settled_within_days NULL, declined_shares, expired_shares); no participant identities.

Competing designs to accept. A single request_events stream with share ids inside; a state table updated transactionally alongside events, if history by date stays reproducible; shares with custom amounts validated by the same invariant.

Bottlenecks and failure modes. One status column per request; shares rounded independently; edits that overwrite the amount; a reminder job reading request-level status; expiry computed at query time with the current rule; full refolding of every request every night at {{requests_per_day}} requests a day; large splits ({{max_participants}} participants) written without a transaction, leaving shares that do not sum.

Incident guidance.

  • One cent short: shares rounded independently. Recompute with the remainder rule, write a correcting version or an adjustment share event (never edit silently), and enforce the invariant at write time with a test on random totals and participant counts.
  • Reminders to people who paid: eligibility must be per share, from share events. Fix the job's selection, add the reminder key, and measure the misfire rate from reminded events followed by earlier paid events.
  • Expired report changed: expiry must use the rule version stored on the request. Backfill rule_version from creation dates and the rules history, restate the report, and add a check that past months do not change when a new rule version is added.

Follow-up guidance. (1) 10000 ÷ 3 = 3333 rem 1: shares 3334, 3333, 3333 by position; Σ = 10000. (2) Two paid events (1000 Monday, 2334 Thursday); Wednesday shows paid 1000, outstanding 2334. (3) The selection above with a NOT EXISTS on reminded events and the idempotency key on (share, reminder number). (4) Candidates should define it: for example, settled when no share is open, with declined shares reported separately, and the denominator as requests created that week. (5) Grain: one row per request (accumulating) plus share events; state as of D from snapshots of open shares and a tail of events.

Rubric anchors. 2: a request with one status and an amount; no partial payments or history. 3: shares and share events, the remainder invariant, state as of D. 4: also edit versions, per-request rule versions, idempotent reminders, conversion recorded once, privacy in analytics, and incident repairs.

Strong signals. Writes the remainder rule and invariant first; defines "settled" with declines explicitly. Red flags. Floats for money; reminders driven by request-level status; analytics that expose who owes whom.

PYP-L3-03.html:
Reference architecture (one defensible design).

  • Identifiers. identifiers (identifier_id, kind email|phone|username, normalised_value, created_at); emails normalised by lower-casing (this exercise's rule), phones to an international format, usernames lower-cased. The raw value lives only here, in the operational store with restricted access.
  • Holdings. identifier_holdings (holding_id, identifier_id, account_id, from_at, to_at NULL, verified_at NULL, end_reason released|lapsed|reassigned_reported|account_closed|removed). At most one verified, open holding per identifier: a partial unique index on (identifier_id) WHERE to_at IS NULL AND verified_at IS NOT NULL, or an exclusion constraint on a range; a concurrent second verification fails and retries against the new state. verification_events (identifier_id, account_id, kind code_sent|confirmed|lapsed, at).
  • Usernames. Holdings of username identifiers carry the release time; available_from = released_at + {{quarantine_days}} days is stored, and a claim before it is rejected.
  • Payments to identifiers. payments (payment_id, sender_account_id, amount_minor, currency, sent_at, recipient_identifier_id, recipient_as_entered_ref, resolved_holding_id NULL, credited_account_id NULL); resolution happens once at send time and is stored. unclaimed_payments (payment_id, identifier_id, deadline_at, rule_version, state waiting|claimed|returned|cancelled, claimed_by_account_id NULL, closed_at NULL) with deadline_at = sent_at + {{claim_window_days}} × 24h under the version in force at send time. Funds set aside by a movement at send time and released by exactly one closing movement.
  • Return job. Selects state = 'waiting' AND deadline_at <= now() from an index on (state, deadline_at); each return is a conditional update … SET state = 'returned' WHERE state = 'waiting' in the same transaction as the money movement, so a retry or a race with a claim cannot apply twice.
  • Analytics. Surrogate identifier ids or a keyed pseudonym (HMAC with a key held outside analytics); fct_unclaimed (payment_id, sent_date, kind, state, claimed_within_window, hours_to_claim, new_account_claimed bool); joins use credited_account_id and the holding at the time, never the current holder.
  • Erasure. Raw values erased from identifiers (or replaced with a tombstone), holdings and payments keep surrogate ids, amounts and times; payments still reconcile.

Competing designs to accept. A bitemporal holdings table; identifiers embedded in an account service with a separate history log, if "who held N on D" is answerable; a token service that maps identifiers to opaque ids.

Bottlenecks and failure modes. Email or phone columns on the user; resolution at read time; lapses never recorded (a stale open holding); deadlines recomputed from dates in UTC; a return job without a conditional update; plain unsalted hashes of phone numbers in analytics (easily reversed by enumerating numbers); reports joined to current holders.

Incident guidance.

  • Payment to a reassigned number reached the previous holder: write the lapse as an event that closes the holding; resolution should require a verified open holding. Identify affected payments from holdings history, handle the money through the support process with an audit trail, and add a monitor for holdings whose verification is older than the rule allows.
  • Returns a day early: use the stored deadline_at instant. Identify payments returned before their deadline, contact and remediate per the product's process, and add a test with deadlines near midnight in several time zones.
  • Report changed after username changes: join via credited_account_id; restate the report and add a check that closed quarters do not change when holdings change.

Follow-up guidance. (1) SELECT account_id, verified_at <= D FROM identifier_holdings WHERE identifier_id = … AND from_at <= D AND (to_at IS NULL OR to_at > D). (2) On the 10th no verified holder: the payment waits as unclaimed with a deadline; on the 20th the new holder verifies and, under this exercise's rule, can claim it within the window. Rows: old holding closed on the 1st (lapsed), unclaimed payment row, new holding from the 20th, claim event. (3) Index on (state, deadline_at); conditional update. (4) credited_account_id joined to account creation dates; the holding at send time. (5) Erase raw values; keep surrogate ids and amounts.

Rubric anchors. 2: identifiers as user columns; resolution at read time. 3: identifier entities, holdings over time with verification, resolution stored, unclaimed state machine with stored deadline. 4: also concurrency on verification, exactly-once returns, keyed pseudonyms, erasure, and incident repairs.

Strong signals. Asks how reassignment is learned and what if it is never reported; stores the deadline. Red flags. Raw identifiers or plain hashes in analytics; resolving the recipient again later; deleting holdings on account closure.

PYP-L3-04.html:
Reference architecture (one defensible design).

  • Purchases (buyer's view). purchases (purchase_id, buyer_account_id, merchant_ref, amount_minor, currency, purchased_at, payment_id), purchase_items (purchase_id, line_no, description, qty, amount_minor), shipment_refs (purchase_id, carrier_ref, tracking_ref, added_at).
  • Rules. programme_rule_versions (rule_version, effective_from, window_days, eligible_categories, evidence_required, seller_response_hours, reopen_days); a claim stores the version in force when it was opened (this exercise's rule), and eligibility at opening is computed against the purchase date and that version.
  • Claims. claims (claim_id, purchase_id, buyer_account_id, reason not_received|not_as_described, amount_claimed_minor, rule_version, opened_at), claim_items (claim_id, line_no). claim_events (event_id, claim_id, kind opened|message|seller_responded|escalated|info_requested|decided|refunded|closed|reopened, actor_role buyer|seller|reviewer|system, at, payload_ref); state and durations derived. Seller deadline opened_at + {{seller_response_days}} × 24h, stored on the opened event or computed from the stored rule version.
  • Messages and evidence. messages (message_id, claim_id, from_role, to_role, sent_at, body_ref); evidence (evidence_id, claim_id, uploaded_by_role, type photo|tracking|document, object_key, content_hash, uploaded_at, delete_after), evidence_visibility (evidence_id, role, granted_at, via_message_id); the seller gets a grant only when the buyer attaches the file to a message to the seller. Files are served by short-lived signed links after a visibility check. delete_after = closed_at + {{evidence_retention_years}} years; after deletion the row keeps type, hash and a deleted_at, so timelines show "evidence removed under retention".
  • Decisions and refunds. decisions (decision_id, claim_id, round 1|2, outcome buyer|seller|partial, refund_minor, reason_codes, rule_version, decided_at); reason codes describe the transaction (for example, tracking showed no delivery), never the person. refunds (refund_id, purchase_id, decision_id, amount_minor, currency, issued_at) with legs back to the funding sources in reverse order; constraint Σ refunds ≤ purchase amount enforced in the issuing transaction. Exponent from currencies; a 30% partial refund is computed in minor units with one stated rounding.
  • Analytics. fct_claim (claim_id, category, opened_month, escalated, first_decision_at, final_decision_at, hours_to_first_decision, outcome, reopened) with the definition of which decision counts written down.

Competing designs to accept. Event sourcing with a state projection; a case-management schema shared with other claim kinds, if the buyer-side visibility and rule versions remain; decisions as events only.

Bottlenecks and failure modes. One overwritten status column; rule lookup at evaluation time with the current version; evidence blobs in the database; visibility enforced only in the UI; refunds in major units or with an assumed exponent; no cap on total refunds; deleting claims along with evidence; at {{claims_per_day}} claims a day, timelines assembled from many tables without an index on claim_id and time.

Incident guidance.

  • Open claims re-evaluated with the new window: eligibility must use the version stored at opening. Restore the stored versions, recompute eligibility for affected claims, correct what buyers saw with a notice, and add a test that a new version does not change any open claim.
  • Refunds 100× too large in an exponent-0 currency: compute in minor units with the exponent from reference data. Stop issuance, quantify affected refunds from the refund table, recover through the defined process with an audit trail, and add a per-currency test and a guard that a refund never exceeds the purchase amount (which would have caught it).
  • Escalation blocked: the deadline counted from the seller's first read. Recompute deadlines from opened_at, allow escalation immediately where due, and measure time to decision from the opened event; add a test for the deadline rule.

Follow-up guidance. (1) Union of events, messages and evidence the buyer may see, ordered by time. (2) A stated rule: for example, first decision for "time to first decision" and final decision for outcomes, both reported. (3) The version in force when the claim is opened (this exercise's rule), with the window measured from the purchase date; a late claim is shown as outside the window with the rule version, not as a judgement. (4) Refund 30% of the purchase in minor units, rounded once; legs in reverse funding order; currency is the purchase currency. (5) Rows keep type, hash and dates; reports use facts, not files.

Rubric anchors. 2: one claims table with a status and a blob column. 3: events, messages, evidence with visibility, decisions with rule versions, refunds capped. 4: also retention with tombstones, deadline rules, refunds against funding legs, careful wording of decisions, and incident repairs.

Strong signals. Separates what the seller can see; fixes the rule version at opening. Red flags. Decisions that label buyers or sellers; evidence visible to all parties; refunds computed in floating point.

PYP-L3-05.html:
Reference solution (PostgreSQL)

WITH originals AS (
  SELECT c.claim_id,
         p.item_category,
         (p.purchased_at AT TIME ZONE b.time_zone)::date AS purchase_day,
         (c.filed_at AT TIME ZONE b.time_zone)::date AS filed_day
  FROM claims c
  JOIN purchases p ON p.purchase_id = c.purchase_id
  JOIN buyers b ON b.buyer_id = p.buyer_id
  WHERE c.reopens_claim_id IS NULL
), judged AS (
  SELECT o.item_category,
         to_char(o.filed_day, 'YYYY-MM') AS claim_month,
         o.filed_day - o.purchase_day AS days_to_claim,
         rule.window_days,
         EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM claims k WHERE k.reopens_claim_id = o.claim_id) AS reopened
  FROM originals o
  CROSS JOIN LATERAL (
    SELECT pr.window_days
    FROM programme_rules pr
    WHERE pr.effective_from <= o.purchase_day
    ORDER BY pr.effective_from DESC
    LIMIT 1
  ) AS rule
)
SELECT item_category,
       claim_month,
       COUNT(*) AS claims,
       COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE days_to_claim > window_days) AS late_claims,
       COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE reopened) AS reopened_claims,
       percentile_cont(0.5) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY days_to_claim) AS median_days_to_claim
FROM judged
GROUP BY item_category, claim_month
ORDER BY item_category, claim_month;

Explanation. Only original claims (reopens_claim_id IS NULL) are counted, so every chain of reopenings counts once and is dated by its original filing, however deep the chain is; no recursion is needed because the original is the one row without a parent. Both timestamps are turned into the buyer's local calendar date with AT TIME ZONE and subtracted as dates, which gives whole calendar days rather than 24-hour periods. The window comes from the rule with the latest effective_from on or before the local purchase date (inclusive, so a purchase on the change date takes the new rule). Late is strictly greater than the window. reopened_claims asks whether any row reopens the claim itself, which keeps two separate claims on one purchase apart.

Complexity. One pass over claims and purchases with hash joins; the lateral rule lookup is a tiny sorted scan per claim (production: an index on effective_from, or validity ranges from LEAD joined by range); the EXISTS is an index lookup on reopens_claim_id. The median is a sort per group.

Dialect notes. Not executed here. Snowflake: CONVERT_TIMEZONE(tz, ts)::date, DATEDIFF('day', a, b), MEDIAN(x) or PERCENTILE_CONT(0.5) WITHIN GROUP, COUNT_IF. BigQuery: DATE(ts, tz), DATE_DIFF(b, a, DAY), PERCENTILE_CONT(x, 0.5) OVER (PARTITION BY …) is analytic only (use APPROX_QUANTILES for an approximate median, or a window and DISTINCT), COUNTIF, and no LATERAL with LIMIT (use a join on validity ranges built with LEAD). Spark SQL: to_date(from_utc_timestamp(ts, tz)), datediff, percentile(x, 0.5) (exact) or percentile_approx. MySQL 8: CONVERT_TZ needs loaded time-zone tables, DATEDIFF, and no built-in median (window with ROW_NUMBER and COUNT). FILTER (WHERE …) is PostgreSQL; elsewhere SUM(CASE WHEN … THEN 1 ELSE 0 END).

Edge cases built into the data. All levels: a claim filed exactly window_days after the purchase (on time) that is reopened after the window and sometimes in a later month; a purchase at about 22:00–23:30 and a claim at about 00:15–02:00 on the day after the window's last day (late by dates, on time by 24-hour periods); reopenings in general. Hard: a rule change during the purchases, a purchase before the change claimed after it with days between the two windows, a purchase on the change date, buyers in several fixed-offset time zones, a Tokyo purchase early in the local morning (the previous date in UTC) filed on the window's last local day, and a Bogota claim filed late in the evening on a month's last day (the next month in UTC). Very Hard: a version with an effective date after every filing (the newest rule must not be used), reopenings of reopenings, and one purchase with two separate original claims of which only the first is reopened.

Common mistakes. Counting every claim row; counting chains once but dated by the latest reopening; EXTRACT(EPOCH …)/86400 or filed_at - purchased_at as an interval truncated to days; >= for lateness; dates in UTC (::date in a UTC session); the rule in force on the filing date; the newest rule; effective_from < purchase_day; mapping reopenings with COALESCE(reopens_claim_id, claim_id) (one level); marking reopened by purchase. Each has a diagnostic.

Follow-up guidance. (1) Add a nullable item_category to programme_rules (NULL = all categories) and prefer the category-specific row: ORDER BY (pr.item_category IS NULL), pr.effective_from DESC, or separate validity ranges per category. (2) A late reopening changes only reopened_claims for the original's month; a time-zone correction can move the purchase date and the claim's month. Materialise per claim (local dates, window, late flag, reopened flag) and aggregate; restate only months whose claims changed, tracked by recorded time. (3) Index claims (reopens_claim_id), claims (filed_at) for monthly slices, programme_rules (effective_from); storing local purchase and filing dates at write time (with the zone used) is reasonable and makes the report cheaper and stable. (4) A CASE on days_to_claim - window_days for late claims; the share's denominator is all claims in the group, stated explicitly.

Rubric anchors. 2: counts every row, or uses 24-hour periods or UTC dates. 3: matches the expected result. 4: also explains restatement, category-specific rules and indexing, and why counting originals is enough without recursion.

Strong signals. Asks which time zone defines a date and which rule version applies before writing SQL. Red flags. Taking the newest rule; counting reopenings; treating lateness as a judgement about the buyer.
